blocks.x: Glycolysis comes from two Greek words: glykys (sweet) and lysis (splitting) — literally, "sugar-splitting." It's a 10-step pathway that converts one molecule of glucose (a six-carbon sugar) into two molecules of pyruvate (a three-carbon compound), and it happens entirely in the cytoplasm of the cell — no mitochondria required to get started.

Think of glucose as a GHC100 note. Most places can't easily "use" a large note directly — the trotro mate can't break it, the roadside seller doesn't have change. So you take it to a money-changing counter. They don't destroy your money — they split it into smaller, more usable notes, and because of how the exchange works, you walk away with a little extra "commission." That commission is your net ATP — the cell's spendable energy currency. Glycolysis is that counter.

sections.title: How does glucose even get into the cell?

blocks.x: Here's a detail most people miss: glucose can't simply slip through the cell membrane on its own. Glucose is water-soluble, but the cell membrane is made of fats and is fat-soluble — and water and oil famously don't mix.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — oil and water at a chop bar

blocks.x: Pour water into oil and watch them separate instead of blending — that's exactly the problem glucose faces at the cell membrane. Because of this mismatch, glucose needs a dedicated "ferry" to get across. That ferry is a protein called a GLUT transporter (Glucose Transporter). GLUT transporters are bidirectional — like a two-way ferry — meaning glucose could technically be carried back out, which is exactly why the very first step of glycolysis "traps" it inside (more on that soon).

blocks.x: There are several types of GLUT transporters, each stationed in different tissues — handy mnemonics help lock these into memory:
Found in the Blood-Brain Barrier, red blood cells, and the fetus. Insulin-independent — the brain and developing baby can't afford to wait for an insulin signal before getting fuel.
Found in the Kidney, Liver, and Pancreas. Insulin-independent, and doubles as a glucose "sensor" — especially in the pancreas, where it helps trigger insulin release.
Found in the Placenta, Neurons, and Kidney. Insulin-independent — neurons need a constant, always-on glucose supply since brain cells rarely store fuel themselves.

Found in Muscle and Fat/adipose tissue. The only insulin-dependent GLUT — insulin increases both the number of GLUT4 transporters at the surface and their efficiency, like a supervisor unlocking extra ferry lanes only when there's a signal to do so.

sections.title: The Preparatory Phase and the Pay-Off Phase

blocks.x: Once inside, glucose goes through 10 steps split into two halves — think of it like starting a small transport business.

Before a trotro driver earns a single cedi, he first has to spend money: fuel, station dues, maybe a small settlement at the lorry park. That's the Preparatory Phase — it costs 2 ATP up front, and it's also where the "vehicle" (glucose) is split into two smaller loads. Only after that investment does the Pay-Off Phase begin — the actual trip, where fares are collected. Each of the two smaller loads pays out separately, which is why the pay-off phase produces 4 ATP total. Subtract the 2 ATP spent up front, and the driver's real profit is net 2 ATP per glucose.

blocks.cap: The whole route in one glance: glucose in at step 1, two pyruvate out at step 10. Darker circles (1, 3, 10) mark the irreversible control points.

blocks.x: A phosphate group is attached to the 6th carbon of glucose to form glucose-6-phosphate, catalyzed by hexokinase (in muscle and most tissues) or glucokinase (in the liver) — the enzyme used depends on the tissue. Both require Mn²⁺ and Mg²⁺ for activity. Analogy: Like getting a wristband stamped at the entrance of an event — once tagged, you can't simply walk back out. Even though GLUT transporters are two-way "ferries," this tag prevents glucose from being carried back out — it's now locked inside the cell.

blocks.title: A simple reshuffle — Isomerization to Fructose-6-phosphate

blocks.x: Phosphoglucose isomerase (also called glucose-6-phosphate isomerase or phosphohexose isomerase) rearranges glucose-6-phosphate into fructose-6-phosphate. Glucose is chemically an aldehyde (an aldose); fructose is a ketone (a ketose) — same atoms, different arrangement of the functional group. This aldose → ketose shift is what lets the next enzyme add a phosphate onto carbon 1, and it also sets the molecule up to be split cleanly into two 3-carbon halves at step 4. Analogy: Like a trotro mate reshuffling passengers to make room, without adding or dropping anyone.

blocks.title: The point of no return — Second Phosphorylation

blocks.x: Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) adds a second phosphate — this time onto carbon 1 — so fructose now carries phosphate groups on both the 1st and 6th carbons, forming fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. Note: "bisphosphate" means the two phosphates sit with carbons in between them, while biphosphate would mean no carbon spacing between them. Analogy: This is the tollbooth where, once you've paid, there's no turning the car around. It's also glycolysis's main regulation checkpoint.

blocks.title: The split — Cleavage into two 3-carbon pieces

blocks.x: Aldolase splits fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into two different 3-carbon molecules: dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (GAP). Analogy: Like splitting one full trotro's cargo into two separate head-loads at the station so two people can carry it onward.

blocks.title: Getting both loads onto the same track — Interconversion

blocks.x: DHAP isn't directly usable further down the pathway, so triose-phosphate isomerase (TPI) converts it into more GAP — meaning both 3-carbon pieces now travel through the exact same remaining steps. Analogy: Like a bank teller converting an old-currency note into the current one so it can be processed at the same counter as everything else.

blocks.title: Energy harvest begins — Oxidation of GAP

blocks.x: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GA3PDH) does two things at once: it adds a phosphate to GAP to form 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, and it uses NAD⁺ to rip off a hydride from GAP, converting NAD⁺ into NADH. Because there are two GAPs (one from each half of the original glucose), 2 NADH are produced in total. Analogy: Like charging a power bank while you're out working — you're storing energy for later, not spending it yet.

Phosphoglycerate kinase transfers the high-energy phosphate from 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate straight onto ADP, forming 3-phosphoglycerate and the pathway's first ATP. Because this happens twice per glucose, 2 ATP are produced here. This is glycolysis's first example of substrate-level phosphorylation. The name says exactly what happens: the phosphate comes directly from the substrate (1,3-bisphosphoglycerate) and is handed straight to ADP by the enzyme. Nothing else is involved — no electron transport chain, no oxygen, no ATP synthase. Why it matters: 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate is an acyl phosphate — a bond so energy-rich that breaking it releases more than enough energy to make ATP, so the transfer is spontaneous and strongly exergonic. Because this route needs no oxygen, it is exactly why glycolysis can keep producing ATP anaerobically — in a sprinting muscle, or in a red blood cell that has no mitochondria at all. Exam point: glycolysis has two substrate-level phosphorylation steps — step 7 (phosphoglycerate kinase) and step 10 (pyruvate kinase) — giving 2 ATP each, so all 4 gross ATP of glycolysis come from substrate-level phosphorylation. Contrast this with oxidative phosphorylation, where ATP is made indirectly, using oxygen and the proton gradient. Analogy: Like a passenger paying the driver directly in cash, on the spot — no bank, no middleman. Oxidative phosphorylation, by contrast, is like waiting for a bank transfer to clear.

Phosphoglycerate mutase switches the phosphate group from the 3rd carbon to the 2nd, forming 2-phosphoglycerate. Analogy: Just moving your load from one shoulder to the other before the final stretch — nothing lost, nothing gained yet.

blocks.title: Loading the spring — Formation of an Enol

blocks.x: Enolase rearranges 2-phosphoglycerate into phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) — an enol (recognizable by its C=C double bond), which holds a lot of tension in its phosphate bond. Analogy: Like winding up a catapult — nothing has fired yet, but a lot of stored energy is ready to release.

blocks.title: The big payout — Final ATP transfer

blocks.x: Pyruvate kinase releases that stored tension, transferring the phosphate from PEP to ADP to form ATP + pyruvate. This happens twice per glucose, for another 2 ATP. We now have 2 pyruvate molecules in total. Analogy: The catapult fires — the biggest, most decisive payment in the whole trip, and it can't be reversed.

sections.title: What's the net profit per glucose?

blocks.x: Remember: steps 6–10 happen twice per glucose, because glucose was split into two 3-carbon pieces back at step 4.

blocks.cap: Spend 2, earn 4, keep 2 — plus 2 NADH "vouchers" saved for the electron transport chain.

blocks.x: Those 2 NADH aren't spent yet — they're like vouchers. If oxygen is available, the cell cashes them in later, where NADH "drops" its hydride to generate a lot more ATP through the electron transport chain. If oxygen is absent, the cell has to recycle NADH differently — covered in the Aerobic vs. Anaerobic section below.

sections.title: Hexokinase vs. Glucokinase — why does the body use two different enzymes for step 1?

blocks.x: Both enzymes catalyze the exact same reaction — phosphorylating glucose — but they behave very differently, and that difference is deliberate.

items.title: Hexokinase — the bodyguard on constant duty

blocks.x: Found in muscle and most other tissues. Has a <term d="Km measures how much substrate is needed for an enzyme to work at half its maximum speed. A LOW Km means the enzyme is highly efficient even at low substrate concentrations.">low Km</term> and low <term d="The maximum speed (rate) an enzyme reaction can achieve when the enzyme is fully saturated with substrate.">Vmax</term> — meaning it works efficiently even when glucose levels are low, but its top speed is capped. It's a <term d="An enzyme that is always present at a steady level in the cell, regardless of changing conditions — it isn't switched on or off in response to signals.">constitutive enzyme</term>, always present at steady levels, because regular tissues always need a baseline capacity to burn glucose. If hexokinase fails, cells like red blood cells can't maintain their energy-dependent shape — and can literally burst.

Found mainly in the liver. Has a high Km and high Vmax — it only kicks into gear when glucose is abundant (like right after a meal), and once active it can process glucose very quickly. It doesn't care if glucose-6-phosphate piles up — its job is simply to clear glucose from the blood to prevent hyperglycemia. Glucokinase is heavily induced by insulin: after eating, insulin signals the liver to manufacture more glucokinase to handle the incoming sugar load. In the pancreas, a related mechanism also makes glucokinase act as the body's glucose sensor, helping trigger insulin release in the first place.

sections.title: How is glycolysis regulated?

blocks.x: Steps 1, 3, and 10 are the pathway's irreversible regulatory steps — run by hexokinase, PFK-1, and pyruvate kinase respectively. These three enzymes act like speed-control valves for the entire pathway; because their reactions can't run backward, controlling them controls the whole flow downstream.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — three checkpoints on the highway

blocks.x: Think of the pathway as a highway with three one-way tollgates. Once a car passes through gate 1, 3, or 10, it can't reverse back through. So if the government (the cell) wants to slow down or speed up traffic on the whole highway, it doesn't try to control every little junction — it just adjusts these three tollgates. That's exactly how the cell keeps tight control over glycolysis without having to micromanage all 10 steps individually.

blocks.cap: Three one-way tollgates — hexokinase, PFK-1, and pyruvate kinase — are where the cell applies the brakes or the accelerator.

blocks.x: The three regulatory steps, one by one

All three are regulated the same basic way: allosteric signals (small molecules that report on the cell's energy status) plus, in the liver, hormonal control through insulin and glucagon. Read each one as answering a single question — does this cell need energy right now?

Reaction: glucose → glucose-6-phosphate (costs 1 ATP). Why regulate here: this is the step that traps glucose inside the cell. Control it and you control whether glucose is committed to any glucose-using pathway at all.

Inhibited by: glucose-6-phosphate — its own product. This is classic feedback (product) inhibition: if G6P is piling up, the pathway downstream is already congested, so there is no sense phosphorylating more glucose.

Note the liver exception: glucokinase (the liver and pancreatic β-cell version) is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate. It has a high Km (low affinity) and high Vmax, so it only works hard when blood glucose is high — exactly what you want in an organ whose job is to mop up excess glucose after a meal. It is induced by insulin. Hexokinase, by contrast, has a low Km (high affinity) so muscle and brain can grab glucose even when levels are low.

Reaction: fructose-6-phosphate → fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (costs 1 ATP). Why regulate here: this is the committed step and the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis — the single most important control point. Glucose-6-phosphate can still escape into other pathways, but once fructose-1,6-bisphosphate is made, the molecule is committed to going all the way to pyruvate.
Activated by: AMP and ADP (signals that the cell is running low on energy), inorganic phosphate (Pi), and above all fructose-2,6-bisphosphate — the most powerful allosteric activator of the enzyme.

Inhibited by: ATP (plenty of energy already — no need to burn more glucose), citrate (the Krebs cycle is full, so fuel is abundant), and H+/low pH (which is why glycolysis slows itself down during lactic acidosis, protecting the cell from acidifying further).

The hormonal layer: fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is made by PFK-2, part of a bifunctional enzyme. Insulin (fed state) activates PFK-2 → more fructose-2,6-bisphosphate → glycolysis speeds up. Glucagon (fasting) triggers phosphorylation that switches the same protein to its FBPase-2 activity → fructose-2,6-bisphosphate falls → glycolysis slows and gluconeogenesis takes over. Note the elegance: one molecule turns glycolysis up and gluconeogenesis down at the same time.

Reaction: phosphoenolpyruvate → pyruvate (makes 1 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation). Why regulate here: it is the final, irreversible step — the exit gate that decides whether the pathway actually finishes.

Activated by: fructose-1,6-bisphosphate — the product of step 3. This is feed-forward activation: if step 3 has opened its gate, step 10 is told in advance to open too, so intermediates don't pile up in the middle of the pathway.

Inhibited by: ATP (energy is plentiful) and alanine (which signals that amino acid building blocks are already abundant, since alanine is made from pyruvate). In the liver, glucagon also triggers phosphorylation of the enzyme, switching it off during fasting so that precious pyruvate is spared for making glucose rather than burning it.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — reading the three gates as one system

blocks.x: Think of the cell as a household deciding whether to cook. Hexokinase asks "is there already food prepared?" (G6P piled up = stop buying ingredients). PFK-1 is the head of the household making the real decision, and it listens to the fullest picture: ATP and citrate say "the pot is full, stand down," while AMP says "we're running on empty, start cooking." Pyruvate kinase is the person at the serving door, opened in advance by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate because the food is already on its way. Notice the pattern that runs through all three: high energy (ATP, citrate) slows glycolysis; low energy (AMP, ADP) speeds it up.

sections.title: What happens when there's "light" (oxygen) vs. "dumsor" (no oxygen)?

blocks.x: Glycolysis itself doesn't require oxygen — but it does need a constant, recycled supply of NAD⁺, which step 6 keeps consuming. What happens to pyruvate and NADH next depends entirely on whether oxygen is around.

blocks.title: Everyday analogy — ECG grid vs. the backup generator

blocks.x: Think of the mitochondria and oxygen supply as the national grid (ECG). When the grid is up (aerobic conditions), NADH is sent to drop its hydride at the electron transport chain, regenerating NAD⁺ and producing a lot more ATP. But when there's dumsor — no oxygen (anaerobic conditions) — the cell switches to a small backup generator: lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) uses the NADH to reduce pyruvate to lactic acid, regenerating NAD⁺ so glycolysis can keep running even without oxygen. It's not as efficient, but it keeps the "lights" (energy supply) from going completely off.

blocks.cap: Both routes solve the same problem — recycling NADH back to NAD⁺ so glycolysis doesn't stall.

blocks.x: Lactic acid produced this way can travel to the liver, where it's converted back into glucose. But if it builds up faster than it can be cleared, it lowers blood pH — making the blood more acidic, a condition called <term d="A build-up of lactic acid in the blood, lowering blood pH and making it more acidic.">lactic acidosis</term>.

blocks.cap: Following the cause-and-effect chain from cell damage to what shows up on a lab report or a scan.

blocks.x: Because <term d="Lactate Dehydrogenase — the enzyme that converts pyruvate to lactate. Its blood levels rise sharply when tissue cells are damaged and spill their contents.">LDH</term> is released when cells are damaged, an abnormally high LDH level in the blood can be a clue pointing toward <term d="Heart attack — death of heart muscle tissue due to lack of blood/oxygen supply.">myocardial infarction</term> (heart attack) — damaged heart muscle cells leak LDH into the bloodstream.

Similarly, if bowel tissue is found to be necrotic (dead), it can point toward <term d="A restriction in blood supply to tissue, causing a shortage of oxygen needed to keep that tissue alive.">ischemia</term> — the tissue was starved of oxygen and blood supply, forcing it into anaerobic metabolism until it could no longer survive.

items.title: Hexokinase failure → red blood cells burst

blocks.x: Red blood cells rely on hexokinase and glycolysis to maintain the ATP needed for their flexible, energy-dependent shape. If this baseline glucose-burning capacity fails, red blood cells can lose their shape and rupture.

Because glucokinase in the liver and pancreas is central to sensing and clearing blood glucose, problems with glucokinase function are linked to blood sugar regulation disorders, including certain forms of diabetes.

sections.title: Key takeaways

items: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, converting glucose into 2 pyruvate, with a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose.
Glucose needs GLUT transporters to cross the fat-soluble membrane, since glucose itself is water-soluble.
GLUT4 (muscle/fat) is the only insulin-dependent transporter; GLUT1, 2, and 3 work independently of insulin.
Steps 1, 3, and 10 are irreversible and serve as the pathway's main regulatory control points.
Hexokinase (low Km/Vmax, constitutive) keeps baseline glucose burning steady in most tissues; glucokinase (high Km/Vmax, insulin-induced) lets the liver mop up large glucose loads after meals.
With oxygen, NADH is reoxidized via the electron transport chain for a large ATP yield; without oxygen, lactate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate to lactic acid to keep glycolysis running.
Clinically, elevated LDH and lactic acidosis can be red flags for conditions like myocardial infarction and tissue ischemia.

lines: "Hexokinase Feeds Pyruvate" — the 3 irreversible/regulated enzymes in order: Hexokinase (step 1), PFK-1 (step 3), Pyruvate kinase (step 10).
"7 and 10 give back" — steps 7 (phosphoglycerate kinase) and 10 (pyruvate kinase) are where ATP is directly produced.
"Glucokinase is Greedy and Generous" — high Km (needs lots of glucose to work = "greedy") and high Vmax (makes a lot when it does = "generous"); liver/pancreas only.
Net yield: 2 ATP + 2 NADH per glucose
Step 3: PFK-1 — F6P → F1,6BP (main control point)
Hexokinase: low Km, low Vmax, inhibited by G6P, most tissues
Glucokinase: high Km, high Vmax, liver/pancreas only

items.d: Fructose-6-P → Fructose-1,6-BP. Uses 1 ATP. Irreversible — main control point.
DHAP ↔ G3P (so both 3-carbon halves become G3P).
